title: Turmoil hits AI buildout as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO
titleJa: Turmoil hits AI buildout as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO
summaryJa: Stock slumps, pulled IPOs and rising spreads on credit default swaps this week sets stage for hyperscaler earnings.
bodyOriginal:
Neoclouds tanked. Credit default swaps soared. Meta turned cash flow negative. And SK Hynix's Solidigm unit canceled plans for its initial public offering.
It's been a rocky week for the AI infrastructure trade.
The Nasdaq followed Thursday's beating with an additional drop on Friday to end the week down 0.7%. Among the hyperscalers, the worst performer was Alphabet, shares of which sank 6% ahead of the internet giant's third-quarter earnings report next week. Microsoft and Amazon are also on the docket, and they each saw shares fall less than 1%.
While the tech market has thus far avoided a dramatic across-the-board sell-off, the artificial intelligence build-out is showing signs of strain.
Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN all fell sharply this week, bringing their losses for October to well over 30% each. CoreWeave, the leader of the pack, has seen spreads on its CDS widen past 11%, generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default.
Meanwhile, yields on the company's 2031 and 2032 unsecured notes topped 15%.
"What investors are doing is throwing every baby out with the bathwater and saying anyone who is a neocloud" will be devalued, Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday.
Fears aren't limited to the U.S. market. Shares of Elice Group, a South Korean cloud provider, dropped 30% in their market debut on Tuesday, and shares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast.
AI optimism has been the major market driver for the past couple of years, as unrelenting demand for new models and services pushes the world's biggest tech companies to spend on infrastructure at historic rates. However, skeptics are getting more vocal in their concerns that returns on AI investment won't justify the capital expenditures.
Analysts at research and advisory firm Gartner predict that 80% of neocloud companies will either cease operations or be absorbed by 2030.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, perhaps the leading AI evangelist remains bullish. Huang said this week at a company conference in Berlin that "demand for the neoclouds is off the charts."
"The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal. "That's going to get solved."
Withdrawn IPO
Wall Street isn't convinced. On Thursday, South Korean memory giant SK Hynix, one of the biggest winners in the AI boom, said it's pulling an IPO for its U.S.-based Solidigm unit, citing market volatility. SK Hynix purchased Solidigm, which makes NAND and SSD storage for data centers, from Intel in 2021.
"While an IPO was expected to ease investment burdens and expand capacity for shareholder returns, the review has been discontinued in light of market conditions and share price trends," SK Hynix said in a release.
Despite the turmoil, all of tech's mega-caps have maintained their investment-grade rating even as they've opened their wallets to fuel their build-outs, including through debt. Even with that group of companies, the market is showing some jitters.
Meta saw its stock plunge 7% on Thursday after the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter of over $2 billion while raising the floor of its full-year capex to $135 billion from $130 billion. Meta also said it plans to spend about $825 billion over the coming years on various leases and contracts, with over $450 billion of those leases being non-cancellable take-or-pay agreements.
Spreads on Meta's five-year CDS reached all-time highs of over 124 basis points. CDS on Nvidia and Oracle also touched records, with their spreads hitting 126 basis points and 343 basis points, respectively, this week. Oracle's stock has lost over one-third of its value this year, and now the company faces risks of a credit rating downgrade.
John Williams, who leads the derivatives practice at law firm Milbank LLP, says investors are seeking numerous ways beyond buying CDS to hedge their bets with respect to the AI trade.
"There's so much investment going into it that it's just very appropriate to look for risk management tools, completely regardless of whether you're bullish or bearish," Williams said. "It would be crazy for people not to be looking for appropriate risk management tools for it."
Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, told CNBC's "SquawkBox Asia" last week that it's "all kind of tied together," referring to AI's impact on the whole market.
"Can you drop a bowling ball in one part of the pool and not get any waves downstream to the rest of the Nasdaq?" he said. "I don't know. I have some concern about that."
— CNBC's Katie Tarasov contributed to this report

title: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
titleJa: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
summaryJa: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?- Published
bodyOriginal:
How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
- Published
Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.
The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.
But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.
Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.
And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.
Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.
But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries?
One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate.
The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.
On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries.
And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes.
If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.
Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care

- Published15 September

- Published29 September
But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows.
However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.
So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK?
Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund.
But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.
But there are two issues to consider.
Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.
And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes).
Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing.
As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.
So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap.
The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.
It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men.
But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.
Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.
So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere.
But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action.
The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.
That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.

title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
titleJa: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
summaryJa: The chancellor will unveil AI spending aimed at shoring up the UK's defences in Wednesday's Budget.
bodyOriginal:
UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
- Published
The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.
As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.
The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.
"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.
"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.
"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."
The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.
But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.
"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.
"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."
The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.
What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?
- Published14 September
Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says
- Published23 hours ago
The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).
Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.
The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.
It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.
It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.
Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.
There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.
But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

title: Moody's holds steady on France's credit rating as country grapples with turmoil and higher yields
titleJa: Moody's holds steady on France's credit rating as country grapples with turmoil and higher yields
summaryJa: Moody's left its credit rating on France at Aa3, giving the country some relief in a week of unrest.
bodyOriginal:
Moody's opted to maintain its credit rating on France as the country contended with a week of civil unrest and rising political risk.
The agency kept France's credit rating at Aa3, a level Moody's still deems "high grade," but it also maintained its negative outlook on the nation.
"The negative outlook reflects the increased risk that the fragmentation of France's political landscape will continue to impair the functioning of the country's legislative institutions," Moody's said in its report.
Moody's noted that it could return France's outlook to stable if its institutions can narrow the deficit.
Investors were anticipating Moody's rating decision as France, the second-largest economy in the euro zone, grappled with protests and a sharp surge in bond yields.
"This political instability, also visible in the current social tensions, risks hampering the French government's ability to address key policy challenges such as an elevated fiscal deficit, rising debt burden, and durable increase in borrowing costs, thus leading to a more rapid weakening in the sovereign's key credit metrics than we currently expect," Moody's said in its report Friday.
This week, the nation's 10-year bond yield surpassed 5% for the first time since 2002. The spread against German bunds is also at a 15-year peak.
Currently, France's deficit-to-GDP ratio is at roughly 5.5% of its GDP, sharply above the 3% limit for member nations in the European Union. The country faces more than $1 trillion of debt that will mature by 2030. Just a month ago, the French finance ministry warned that the nation's debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to hit 121.7% in 2027.
At the same time, France has been rocked by protests. Last weekend, more than 500,000 people marched to express their frustration against declining public services and high costs of living.
S&P Global and Fitch cut their ratings on France in 2025.

title: Trump dropping some Canada tariffs but 'replacing' them with other products
titleJa: Trump dropping some Canada tariffs but 'replacing' them with other products
summaryJa: Sen. Susan Collins announced Canada was dropping Canadian tariffs, but the White House later said it was "replacing" the ones removed from the list.
bodyOriginal:
The White House on Friday said it would drop tariffs on some Canadian goods, but replace them with other products from the major U.S. trade partner.
The move was revealed after Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, took credit for pushing the Trump administration to issue tariff exemptions on several categories of Canadian imports she says are "crucial" for her state's industries.
But Collins' announcement, which The Wall Street Journal first reported, did not mention that while tariffs would be removed for some Canadian products, new ones would be added to the list of goods subject to steep U.S. duties. The White House announced the new tariffs less than an hour after Collins touted the new exemptions to the tariffs, which are unpopular in the state where she's fighting for reelection.
President Donald Trump earlier Friday signed a proclamation "removing certain products" from the list of items that he slapped 50% tariffs on over the summer using a 96-year-old trade law.
But he is "replacing those products with certain valves, carpets, waste products, and others," according to a White House fact sheet detailing the proclamation.
The changes are being made to "further refine the scope of the tariffs on certain Canadian products," according to the fact sheet, which does not mention Maine.
The new additions and removals from the list of goods covered by the "Section 338" tariffs will take effect Oct. 30, four days before the Nov. 3 U.S. election, the fact sheet said.
Asked what Collins had agreed to in her conversations pushing Trump administration officials for lower tariffs on products affecting her state, her spokeswoman Phoebe Keller told CNBC that the senator "requested exemptions for products that are important to Maine and will continue to do so."
Before the fact sheet was made public, Collins' office sent a press release crediting the senator with securing the new tariff exemptions on "nine categories of products crucial for Maine's agricultural industries."
That announcement came as voters have already started casting ballots in the pivotal Maine Senate race, where Trump's unpopular tariffs have been a top issue.
Collins' Democratic opponent, fifth-generation Maine logger Troy Jackson, quickly pushed back, insisting Collins deserves blame for enabling Trump's tariff policies.
"Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire," Jackson said in a statement.
Trump has slapped heavy tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods during his second term as president as he has escalated a trade war against the top U.S. economic partner. Many of those tariffs have put considerable strain on businesses in Maine, which imports far more products from Canada than from any other country.
White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC in a statement Friday afternoon that Trump's latest tariff proclamation is part of his efforts to "address Canada's discriminatory treatment of U.S. commerce."
"The President is taking action in response to Canada's continued discrimination against and additional retaliation targeting U.S. commerce, with the goal of protecting American farmers, manufacturers, and workers," said Middleton. "This administration will continue to use every available tool to restore reciprocity in our bilateral trade relationships and safeguard the economic prosperity and national security of the American people."
Collins has previously touted her efforts to push back on the president's protectionist trade policies. In the first televised debate between Collins and Jackson on Oct. 6, the GOP incumbent took credit for removing some items from Trump's list of tariffs on Canadian goods, including road salt.
Jackson fired back, "What about everything else? We can't eat road salt."
In her press release Friday, Collins said she has asked U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "for tariff relief" for the Maine-centric products, stressing the "burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families."
"I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally and largest trading partner," she said.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, Mexico is the largest U.S. trading partner.
The products being exempted from the Section 338 tariffs include corrugated paper, plastic boxes and packing bags, refrigeration equipment, multiple forms of machinery and seaweed and algae products, according to Collins.

title: White House says the US is lifting tariffs on some Canadian goods
titleJa: White House says the US is lifting tariffs on some Canadian goods
summaryJa: Susan Collins, a Republican in a tight race to keep her senate seat in next month's elections, said she had been working with the White House on tariff relief.
bodyOriginal:
White House says the US is lifting tariffs on some Canadian goods
- Published
The US is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, with the White House saying on Friday it was working to "protect the economic prosperity and national security of the American people".
The exemptions could also boost Republican candidates in the midterms elections on 3 November, as many US voters list affordability and economic pressures as top issues.
Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race in Maine to keep her seat in the election, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.
After trade talks collapsed this summer, the US and Canada started an escalating tariff war that has affected both sides of the border.
The White House, in a statement, said that starting 30 October the US would remove certain products from the list of Canadian goods it taxes, such as plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes.
It added those items would be replaced with certain valves, carpets, waste products, among others.
The White House said the action reflects President Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade", as well as "offsetting the burden and disadvantage on U.S. commerce from Canada's discriminatory treatment".
The BBC has contacted the White House, US commerce department and trade representative for further comment.
Also on Friday, President Donald Trump said that Canada is "working very hard" on a trade deal with the US.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday that Canada is open to a mutually beneficial deal, but is willing to wait it out.
"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said, according to CBC.
Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met with members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.
So far, Canada has not commented on the White House's announcement.
LeBlanc's office did not immediately respond on Friday to the BBC's request for comment.
The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts
- Published31 August
The Wall Street Journal had reported that the exemptions, largely focused on Canadian agricultural and forestry, were made in a bid to help Collins and other Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections.
The reductions could be offset by raising levies on other Canadian goods, the Journal reported.
In a statement Collins put out before the White House announcement, the incumbent lawmaker, who is trying to clinch her sixth term, said she had "secured additional tariff exemptions products crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".
"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," she posted on X.
Collins said she has asked US officials and senior administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada.
Maine's economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the month-long trade war.
Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.

title: Scalpers offer Apple iPhone Duo buyers hundreds extra outside Beijing launch
titleJa: Scalpers offer Apple iPhone Duo buyers hundreds extra outside Beijing launch
summaryJa: Apple's global launch of the foldable iPhone Duo brought scalpers to the Beijing flagship store looking to pay big for the already pricey devices.
bodyOriginal:
The iPhone Duo has an eye-popping price tag, but initial interest in Apple's first foldable phone in China appears solid.
On the day of the global launch on Friday, scalpers like Alex Wang stood outside the flagship store in Beijing's popular shopping area, Sanlitun, offering to pay customers an extra 3,000 Chinese yuan ($448) to buy their newly purchased phones on the spot.
"I feel the Duo can be sold with a higher price for half a month," he told CNBC while watching the lines of Duo customers who had pre-booked their phones. "The main reason is the tight supply."
Though foldables are still a niche product globally, China's market is the single largest, according to Counterpoint Research.
Apple fan Mary Tong, who was first in a line of about 100 people at the Sanlitun store, showed up at 6 a.m. to pick up her foldable device.
"Apple has been the laggard," she said. "I think many Chinese do prefer foldable phones."
Huawei is promoting its own AI assistant XiaoYi to boost the Chinese smartphone maker's competitiveness against Apple and other homegrown rivals. Huawei, which already has a broad lineup of foldable phones, launched a new trifold called the Mate XT2 that is priced at about $3,000 on Sept. 7, two days before Apple's Duo announcement.
China's Xiaomi unveiled its own pricey foldable, the 18 Fold, around the same time.
Even before the Beijing Apple store's regular opening hours, customers without a reservation showed up to test their luck to get their hands on the new phone. Apple had said the Duo would not be available for walk-in purchase on launch day in mainland China and would be "limited" in other countries. Each online purchase was restricted to two phones.
Zhang Zheng said he had tried to order one on the site but was discouraged by the delivery timeline, which stretched to January 2027. He said he still wants to buy one.
"I think it will be useful for work and it's cool to look at," he said.
While there was buzz about the device itself, expectations for Apple Intelligence were negligible. The company said a version of the AI system is set for beta testing this month for the mainland China market and will include features like live translation, Clean Up in photos, and writing tools.
On Oct. 14, Beijing approved Alibaba AI models for use in Duo and other Apple devices as part of the U.S. tech giant's pending AI rollout in the country. Apple received Chinese regulatory clearance over the summer.
Chinese official media cited ex-CEO Tim Cook on a recent China trip as saying Apple's revamped Siri AI would not be available in the country yet.
Duo customer John Zhao said he had tried Apple Intelligence while working overseas, and it was "nice but not beyond imagination." He expects the Chinese version to be less exciting.

title: Trump's executive order targets mortgage insurance, refinance costs. What it means for borrowers
titleJa: Trump's executive order targets mortgage insurance, refinance costs. What it means for borrowers
summaryJa: Trump's executive order on housing aims to lower mortgage costs. Here's what it means for homeowners and buyers.
bodyOriginal:
President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that aims to reduce mortgage costs as rising interest rates and inflation make homeownership less affordable.
The order, titled "Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People," directs federal agencies to proactively cancel mortgage insurance on eligible future loans and expand a program to make refinancing cheaper, among other actions.
In an X post on Thursday, Federal Housing Finance Agency director Bill Pulte said "millions of Americans will save thousands and thousands of dollars."
But it's difficult to know the future consumer impact without more details, according to Keith Gumbinger, vice president of mortgage website HSH.
Trump's executive order comes less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with rising costs and housing affordability a major concern among voters. It builds on previous orders to restrict Wall Street firms from buying single-family homes, among other actions.
Homeownership has become less affordable in recent years. In 2025, the monthly payment for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage on a median-priced home was roughly 33% of the median family's income, up from 26% in 2022, according to the Federal Reserve's latest Survey of Consumer Finances published in early October.
Whether you're a current homeowner or future buyer, here are some of the key things to know about the new executive order.
Mortgage insurance changes
Conventional loans — mortgages not insured or backed by U.S. government programs — typically require private mortgage insurance, or PMI, when a down payment is less than 20% of the home's purchase price. By contrast, Federal Housing Administration mortgages require mortgage insurance on all loans.
Trump's executive order directs the FHFA to create a pilot program that cancels eligible borrowers' mortgage insurance "proactively" once their home equity reaches a certain threshold, according to the White House. This would apply to mortgages originated after the pilot program launches.
Currently, conventional loan borrowers can generally remove PMI once their loan balance is below 80% of the purchase price or once they have reached 20% equity, according to Fannie Mae. Once your balance is below 80%, you can ask your loan servicer if you're eligible to remove PMI, or they may remove it automatically when your balance reaches 78% of the original value.
In a statement Thursday, Seth Appleton, president of U.S. mortgage insurers, an industry trade organization, said: "We commend the President's focus on lowering costs for future homeowners, and the private mortgage insurance industry is proud to already be delivering on that goal."
Typically, the cost of PMI can be 0.2% to 2% of the loan annually, but varies based on your down payment size, credit score, amount borrowed and other factors, according to Fannie Mae.
For example, if you purchased a $600,000 home with a 10% down payment and a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 7.3%, your monthly mortgage insurance could be $351, according to a private mortgage calculator from Freddie Mac.
"Most mortgages ... are carrying PMI at this point in time, especially with the way home prices have been and down payments being as small as they've been in recent years," Gumbinger said.
During the second quarter of 2026, the median home down payment was 13.7% of the home's purchase price, or $27,100, according to a September report from Realtor.com.
Mortgage refinancing costs
Trump's executive order also aims to reduce mortgage refinancing costs by making permanent the FHFA's pilot program that waives the lender's title insurance policy and allows "cost-friendly alternatives," according to the White House.
"I don't know that it's necessarily a game-changer in terms of the cost of housing, which is dictated by home price and mortgage rates at the moment," Gumbinger said. "But you know, every little bit certainly helps."
As of Oct. 23, mortgage interest rates for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages were 7.32%, according to Freddie Mac, and refinance demand was down 59% in mid-October, compared to the same week the previous year.
Originally planned through November 2027, the FHFA pilot was "limited in scope," for refinances with a loan-to-value ratio below 80%, in a handful of states, former FHFA director Sandra Thompson said during a Congressional hearing in April 2024.
Thompson estimated that consumers could save $500 to $1,500 in closing costs for loans sold under the pilot program.
Making the program permanent could save borrowers because the lender's title insurance policy, which is usually required for new loans and refinances, "has always been fairly pricey," Gumbinger said.
The lender's title and title insurance-related fees generally make up the largest share of mortgage closing costs, according to a 2025 Urban Institute report.

title: Meta shares are down 9% this week. Here's why Mike Khouw is buying now
titleJa: Meta shares are down 9% this week. Here's why Mike Khouw is buying now
summaryJa: Meta shares just had their worst week in four years. Here's why Mike Khouw is buying now
bodyOriginal:
Size is a relative matter. The standard Manhattan apartment would seem almost claustrophobic compared to the vast expanses offered by suburban living. A similar dynamic is playing out in the market.
Mega-cap companies are generally defined as those with market capitalizations exceeding $200 billion. Of course, the largest companies are another order of magnitude larger than that. For example, Meta, which reported stellar earnings this week, has a current market capitalization of $1.65 trillion.
But concerns about its AI buildout expenses wiped $135 billion from its market cap in just four sessions, or put another way, roughly the value on and entire Uber. Market cap is one way to understand how big these companies are, but another is by examining the size of their operations, and their opportunities.
Consider Muse.
Meta's personal AI agent is designed to be more of an active digital assistant than a conventional conversational chatbot. Muse can open browsers, fill out forms, send emails, schedule appointments, book travel, and (potentially) even make purchases.
To understand how large an economic opportunity this represents for the company, consider what something like that might be worth. $5 per month per user? (Not in subscription fees necessarily, mind you, just monetizable economic value). That seems a bit low for something so powerful. $10/month? Quite realistically. Then consider the size of Meta's ecosystem's daily active user base across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. That number is truly "mega": 3.6 billion, supposedly counting each person only once. If we assume that each of those individuals has and uses a global phone - 5.86 billion unique people on the planet do - that means Meta interacts at least once with 61.4% of them each day.
If Muse is worth $120/year and reaches just 1% of Meta's Daily Active People, that's $4.3 billion/year. If it's worth half that amount, but reaches 20% of their daily actives, that's $43.2 billion/year. The first number seems absurdly low as a back-of-the-napkin figure, but the $135 billion valuation loss in less than a week is offset by $20 billion in revenue (the company trades at just under 7x revenue). If Muse can generate $30 billion in revenues, it is a megacap company in its own right!
So why has the company sold off if everything is so rosy? A massive $25 billion lawsuit in New Mexico, a potential PR headache related to a deal struck between the company and its founder to resolve potential tax liabilities associated with a possible billionaire's tax in California that preserves his voting rights, and, of course, concerns about debt, on the balance sheet and off, to finance the enormous investment that the company is making (and expanding) in AI, and AI jitters generally. title: Qatar deal to buy U.S. natural gas shows how Iran war has redrawn global energy markets
titleJa: Qatar deal to buy U.S. natural gas shows how Iran war has redrawn global energy markets
summaryJa: The Iran war is transforming global energy markets and benefiting U.S. companies, especially liquefied natural gas exporters.
bodyOriginal:
Before the Iran war, Qatar was one of the biggest natural gas exporters in the world. After only eight months, the Gulf state is now buying supplies from its principal competitor — the United States.
QatarEnergy struck a deal Thursday with U.S. exporter Cheniere Energy to buy 4 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas, or LNG, annually through 2054. The purchase price is indexed to the U.S. Henry Hub price plus a fixed fee. Deliveries are expected to begin in the 2030s.
"We look forward to reliably supplying QatarEnergy from both Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi into the second half of this century," Cheniere CEO Jack Fusco said in a statement.
The gas that Doha will buy is less than 1% of the global LNG trade of more than 400 million metric tons. But "in terms of an individual deal, this is about as big as you see in the U.S," said Alex Munton, director of global gas and LNG at Rapidan Energy in Houston.
The deal signals how the Iran war is reshaping global energy markets to the benefit of U.S. companies, cementing the dominance of American LNG exporters. Shares of Cheniere and Venture Global, the other independent U.S. player, have gained 26% and 40%, respectively, since the start of the war.
Qatar knocked out
Qatar was second only to the U.S. in LNG exports before the war. But shipments have since collapsed in the eight months since Iran bombed its key production facility at Ras Laffan. The attack badly damaged two production lines, taking out about 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity.
It will take about three years to repair the damage at Ras Laffan, Qatar's energy minister, Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, has said. The Persian Gulf state has declared force majeure — citing unexpected, uncontrollable events preventing contracts from being honored — every month since the March attack.
"It did give us a big blow, if you will, for our production capability for the next few years," Al-Kaabi said in an interview on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in September. Qatar is exporting "very little" LNG right now because "we can't export through the Hormuz Strait," he said.
"Very sparingly, some ships are crossing the straits but a very small amount, it's not something that would even be measurable in a percentage point," the energy minister said.
Freedom of navigation
And it is far from clear what security conditions in Hormuz will look like when the repairs are done at Ras Laffan. The decades-long contract with Cheniere indicates that Qatar sees a risk that freedom of navigation will never return to Hormuz as Iran keeps attacking tankers, Munton said.
It is harder to find ways to get around Hormuz in the case of LNG because it is fundamentally a waterborne product, the analyst said.
"It's liquefied so it can be put on a ship and that requires access to seaborne routes," Munton said. "They've got to access the Strait of Hormuz. There's no other way of getting LNG to market. They're just stuck."
With its production badly damaged and Hormuz blocked off, QatarEnergy is expanding its LNG trading business through the Cheniere deal, Munton said.
It secured a $3 billion loan earlier this month from Chinese banks that could allow it to secure more U.S. LNG to honor its international delivery commitments, said Manav Gupta, a UBS analyst, in a note to clients Thursday.
Bullish Wall Street
Venture Global, for example, is in advanced talks with QatarEnergy to supply 3 million metric tons annually, unnamed sources told Reuters.
With the Qatar deal, Cheniere is disproving the bears' case that it will struggle to secure incremental sales which would in turn constrain capacity expansion, Gupta said. UBS has a stock price target of $340 on Cheniere, implying 18% upside from Thursday's close.
Wall Street is broadly bullish on both Cheniere and Venture Global. Nearly 90% of equity analysts who cover Cheniere rate it a buy, with an average price target of $314, implying about 9% upside from Thursday's close.
Nearly 60% of analysts recommend Venture Global as a buy with the rest rating it a hold. The average price target of $17 would amount to some 35% upside from Thursday's close.
"The U.S. once again is being called on by buyers to diversify supply," Munton said. "So much is under construction in the U.S. that you get to the point where now the U.S. is becoming disproportionately big in terms of global [LNG] market share."

title: Fewer people are flying as airfare soars. Here's why airlines aren't worried
titleJa: Fewer people are flying as airfare soars. Here's why airlines aren't worried
summaryJa: Airlines are reporting fewer people flew in the third quarter as airfare surged on fuel costs, but executives say travelers are mostly swallowing higher fares.
bodyOriginal:
Fewer people are flying this year, but with airfare this high and climbing, airline executives say that's just fine.
The number of people screened at U.S. checkpoints is on track for its first annual decline since 2020. Major U.S. carriers have said capturing higher fares is more important than fully filling their planes or flying record numbers of travelers.
"We're actively prioritizing yield versus load factor and really happy as we see it. It fits right in with the premium investments that we're making," American Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said on the company's earnings call Thursday.
American's load factor, a gauge of how full planes are flying, fell to 83.4% in the third quarter from 86% in the same quarter of 2025.
Fares keep climbing
The price of plane tickets has skyrocketed as airlines grapple with a spike in jet fuel prices, their biggest expense after labor, and pass more of those costs on to customers.
Fares in September were up more than 22% from a year earlier, according to the latest inflation read. Fare tracker Hopper said it expects this holiday season to come with the most expensive ticket prices in years.
The average Southwest Airlines fare in the third quarter, for example, was $231.69, up close to $50 from a year earlier. That doesn't include Southwest's new fees, like its extra charges for checked bags or a seat closer to the front of the plane.
The airline's count of revenue passengers, however, fell 3.2% from a year ago, to about 33.5 million people.
Still, both fares and the passenger counts exceeded Southwest's expectations.
"Passenger fares came in about $3 above what our forecast was and the more important thing is that passenger volumes also exceeded our expectations," Southwest CEO Bob Jordan said on an earnings call Thursday.
Since April — when airlines began warning in earnest about profits taking a hit from the spike in jet fuel — through Thursday, about 9.3 million fewer people were screened at airport checkpoints compared with the same period of 2025, according to the Transportation Security Administration. While that's down less than 2% from last year, it follows years of growth.
With jet fuel prices more than double year-ago levels — as seen in U.S. Gulf Coast spot prices going for $4.63 a gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration — airlines have been focused on recovering as much of the fuel spike as possible.
Even despite some drops, airline executives said during their earnings calls that travel demand overall is robust, especially for profitable premium cabins like business class.
And not every carrier is seeing a decline. United Airlines flew 2.4% more passengers in the third quarter than it did a year ago, and said its unit revenue rose by 16%, the biggest increase since the pandemic.
"I've been pleasantly surprised at the industry's ability this year to raise yields and pass through much of the increase in fuel prices," CEO Scott Kirby said on the company's earnings call Wednesday. "So it's possible that airlines will continue to focus on yields at the expense of load factor and that alone could get us to double-digit margins next year."
Profit hit
Most airlines are anticipating that fuel costs will continue to bite, but executives say they're confident in their pricing power.
United, for example, said it expects to pay an average of $4.80 a gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from an average price of $3.90 a gallon in the third.
American, United, Delta Air Lines and Southwest all cut their profit forecasts for 2026 this month when they reported earnings. American is the only one of the four that expects to post a loss this year.
American and others have also reduced growth plans or warned the industry could dial back on its goals for expanding capacity, which could keep fares elevated. Reduced capacity can make bookable seats scarcer, driving up prices even more if demand holds.
The carriers said demand has been particularly strong for premium seats, which command hundreds, if not thousands of dollars, more than coach tickets.
Smaller airlines set to report results in the coming weeks, including Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air, have traditionally focused on more price-sensitive customers, which could show if those travelers are pulling back at all.
One factor that could also affect air travel is the demise of Spirit Airlines, which went out of business in early May.
"Some of its customers have likely stopped flying," Bank of America said in a research note Thursday.

title: AI's 'Black October': Critical PHP flaws set off global security scramble
titleJa: AI's 'Black October': Critical PHP flaws set off global security scramble
summaryJa: Governments and businesses around the globe are scrambling to contain the fallout after the PHP vulnerabilities leaked online.
bodyOriginal:
Cybersecurity teams around the globe are rushing to patch PHP programming language flaws this week, in an artificial intelligence safety moment that's being described as "Black October."
Nearly 70% of all websites use PHP, according to some estimates.
"In the last 2 days there have been several dozen cyber attacks which, in isolation, would each have been the worst to happen in an entire calendar year," John Milinovich, senior director of product management at Figma, wrote in a post on X on Thursday. "Every sector from government to education to big tech and banks is being massively affected, and people are starting to freak out."
Researchers at Google's Wiz and the AI firm Calif discovered major vulnerabilities in PHP in August by using advanced AI models from OpenAI and Google. But by Tuesday, the warnings had spread online, prompting governments and businesses around the globe to scramble to contain the fallout.
Major AI companies have been warning about the technology's advancing cybersecurity capabilities since April, when Anthropic announced a limited rollout of its powerful model called Mythos. Concerns mounted in July, when OpenAI disclosed that two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached a company called Hugging Face.
Experts believe the PHP security flaws serve as the latest example of what's to come.
Jason Clinton, deputy chief information security officer at Anthropic, wrote in a post on X on Thursday that the cybersecurity landscape is likely to get "a lot worse" before it gets better.
"Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now," Clinton said. "Not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)"
While many large companies have access to advanced models that they can use to harden their systems, serious bugs could be more challenging for small- and medium-sized businesses to address, Chris Krebs, former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, told CNBC on Friday. He encouraged smaller companies to "constantly" scan for vulnerabilities, deploy patches as fast as possible or take legacy systems offline.
"This is a significant week or two in cybersecurity," Krebs told CNBC's "Squawk Box." "As I mentioned, 3% of all critical vulnerabilities ever discovered have been found in the last month."
Figma's Milinovich encouraged individuals to set up two-factor authentication for "everything," use a password manager, set up an identity protection app and move smart devices to their own network. He added that people should lean in and experiment with AI to understand how powerful the tools have become.
"While I still firmly believe that AI will be a net positive for humanity, it's more clear to me than ever that the societal and individual risk is very real, and is playing out NOW," Milinovich said.
Krebs added that company leaders and employees should check in on their security teams.
"Make sure they're doing okay," he said. "They've had a heck of a week."
—CNBC's Isabel O’Brien contributed to this report

title: Doctors call Moderna, Merck cancer vaccine data a major advancement — despite Wall Street reaction
titleJa: Doctors call Moderna, Merck cancer vaccine data a major advancement — despite Wall Street reaction
summaryJa: Six melanoma specialists said the Moderna and Merck vaccine results represent a clinically meaningful result for melanoma patients who underwent surgery.
bodyOriginal:
Leaked confidential data. A major stock sell-off.
Beneath the chaos surrounding Moderna and Merck's latest data on their personalized cancer vaccine, oncologists see something else: an important milestone in melanoma treatment.
The companies on Thursday released detailed results from a Phase 3 trial on their mRNA-based shot after partial data leaked on social media platforms earlier that day.
The vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% when given alongside Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda, compared with Keytruda alone. The combination also reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy, according to the trial on roughly 1,100 patients whose tumors were removed by surgery.
The stock market's reaction contrasted with the assessment of six melanoma specialists, who told CNBC the results represent a clinically meaningful advance that could eventually become a standard of care for patients who undergo surgery first and have not received immunotherapy before their operation.
"This has the potential to be a major breakthrough in melanoma treatment and also cancer immunotherapy in general that will open the door to greater outcomes for patients," said Dr. Sekwon Jang, a melanoma specialist at Inova Schar Cancer and principal investigator at one of the trial's U.S. sites.
Dr. Janice Mehnert, NYU Langone skin cancer specialist and trial investigator, added that "this is the first time we're seeing that when you add something to immunotherapy, you actually boost the efficacy of the immunotherapy."
The vaccine is not far from potentially entering the market for the first time and reaching melanoma patients. In an interview ahead of the results, Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said the company is finishing a filing with regulators as it aims to get the drug fully approved next year.
"It's a very, very happy moment for the field, for patients," he said.
Major advance in melanoma
An immunotherapy like Keytruda wakes up the immune system to detect and attack cancer cells. Unlike preventative vaccines, which protect against infections that can cause cancer, Moderna and Merck's treatment acts like a blueprint to train the immune system to recognize and hunt residual cancer cells based on the specific mutations in an individual patient's tumor.
The significance of the Phase 3 data extends beyond delaying a recurrence, doctors said. Melanoma can become much more difficult to treat when it returns after surgery and spreads to distant parts of the body, such as the lungs, brain or liver. Patients with advanced disease may require additional treatments, including immunotherapy, radiation or further surgery, and those methods are not guaranteed to work.
Preventing the cancer from returning could spare patients from ever facing the risks and complexities of metastatic disease altogether.
"If we can essentially cure more patients with earlier-stage melanoma and never have to deal with unresectable metastatic disease — that's a wonderful advance," said Dr. Michael Postow, chief of the Melanoma Service at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and an investigator on the trial.
Ideally, patients in the future may be able to undergo surgery and receive the vaccine and Keytruda without needing further melanoma treatment, Postow told CNBC.
Still, questions remain about whether the combination ultimately helps patients live longer, what the benefit looks like over longer periods of time and which patients benefit most.
The results also leave open where the personalized vaccine would fit into a changing melanoma treatment landscape, some experts said.
The trial tested the vaccine after surgery, alongside Keytruda, rather than against immunotherapy regimens given before surgery. That's an approach increasingly used for eligible patients with resectable melanoma, where the primary tumor can be removed. The data do not show that using the vaccine approach is more or less effective than receiving immunotherapy before surgery.

title: DOJ sues to block Alaska from certifying Senate race winner if Republican narrowly loses
titleJa: DOJ sues to block Alaska from certifying Senate race winner if Republican narrowly loses
summaryJa: The Alaska race is one of several contests around the United States that could determine whether Republicans retain their slim majority in the Senate
bodyOriginal:
The Department of Justice filed an extraordinary lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying the winner of its upcoming U.S. Senate election if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
The lawsuit cites what it suggests is likely voter confusion from having another candidate, named Daniel J. Sullivan, on the ballot and the chance that could help Democratic nominee Mary Peltola win what is expected to be a close contest between her and the incumbent Sullivan.
The DOJ is asking a judge to bar Alaska from certifying "any result that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
The Alaska race is one of several Senate contests around the United States that could determine whether Republicans retain their slim majority in the upper chamber of Congress. Alaska's general election for the Senate is conducted by ranked-choice voting. Voters rank their candidates in order of preference.
"Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan — whose candidacy, Defendant Beecher [Alaska Elections Director Carol Beecher] found, is 'for the purpose of confusing or misleading voters and compromising the fairness of the ballot' — the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election," the suit in U.S. District Court in Alaska says.
"The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska," says the suit, which names the state, Beecher, Alaska's Election Boards, and the state Ballot Counting Review Board as defendants.
CNBC has requested comment from the DOJ, both Sullivans and Peltola about the suit.
The suit says that "the sole purpose" of the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan "is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan." The suit says Daniel J. Sullivan decided to run as a Republican "with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him."
Daniel J. Sullivan received just 2.5% of the vote in Alaska's open primary on Aug. 28, but that was enough to win him one of four spots on the Senate general election ballot.
Peltola got 49.5% in the primary, and Sen. Sullivan received 41.1%. Another Republican, Gerald Heikes, received just 1.1% of the primary vote, earning him the fourth spot on the ballot.
Although Daniel J. Sullivan sought to run as a Republican, the Division of Elections decided not to list that party next to his name on the general election ballot. Both Sen. Sullivan and Heikes have the words "registered Republican" next to their name on the ballot.
In its suit, the DOJ said, "Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot threatens to mislead Alaskan
citizens who want to vote for Senator Sullivan."
"For example, some supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan," the suit says.
"Other supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will be confused as to how to rank the three Republican candidates as to defeat Peltola. They might not rank Senator Sullivan at all, resulting in votes for Daniel J. Sullivan to be transferred to Peltola after Daniel J. Sullivan's all-but-guaranteed elimination in the first or second round of tabulations."
The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the Alaska Senate race as one of seven "toss-up" contests for that chamber.
FiftyPlusOne's average of polling in the race shows Peltola, the former U.S. House member from Alaska, with a narrow two-point lead over Sullivan.

title: TikTok U.S. hunts for multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources tell CNBC
titleJa: TikTok U.S. hunts for multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources tell CNBC
summaryJa: The operator of the social media platform in the U.S. has sounded out opportunities to obtain capacity over the coming years.
bodyOriginal:
TikTok's U.S. entity is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources told CNBC, amid a global scramble for digital infrastructure deals.
The company, officially TikTok USDS Joint Venture, operates the social media platform in the U.S. and has sounded out opportunities to obtain capacity over the coming years, two people familiar with the discussions, who asked to remain anonymous as they weren't authorized to share the information, told CNBC.
TikTok U.S. is looking for four gigawatts of compute power by the early 2030s, one source said.
Companies across the world are looking to secure more compute capacity as artificial intelligence workloads become more prominent.
A company spokesperson told CNBC that the company "runs primarily on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in the U.S. and Oracle will continue to be our primary cloud infrastructure provider."
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, or OCI, typically runs in facilities that Oracle leases. CNBC has approached Oracle for comment.
There are signs TikTok U.S.' product plans could require extra compute going forward.
The company has numerous machine learning roles live on its website. A job advert posted by TikTok states that the company is "shipping a flagship B2B AI product at the frontier of large-model inference and creative automation."
TikTok U.S. localizes algorithm training
TikTok USDS Joint Venture was established in 2026 in compliance with U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order mandating the divestiture of TikTok in the U.S. from its Chinese parent company, ByteDance.
In January, TikTok U.S. said it would "retrain, test, and update" its prized recommendation algorithm, which is built on machine learning, on U.S. user data. The company's recommendation algorithm will be "secured in Oracle's U.S. cloud environment," it said.
TikTok U.S. has three managing investors, Silver Lake, Oracle and MGX, each holding 15%. The Dell Family Office, the investment firm of Michael Dell, is also an investor. ByteDance retained 19.9% of the new entity.

title: Civil servant who juggled five jobs says he was 'surprised' to be charged with fraud
titleJa: Civil servant who juggled five jobs says he was 'surprised' to be charged with fraud
summaryJa: Kashim Chowdhury denied being dishonest when not telling employers he had other jobs.
bodyOriginal:
Civil servant who juggled five jobs says he was 'surprised' to be charged with fraud
- Published
A civil servant accused of fraudulently juggling multiple government jobs says he was ''surprised'' to have been charged with fraud.
Kashim Chowdhury told the jury at Southwark Crown Court he had not been dishonest in failing to tell his employers he had other government jobs.
"At that time I was just on auto pilot, I was like a robot, I was not thinking clearly," he said.
Chowdhury, 55, from east London, is accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.
Between 2020 and 2023 Chowdhury had eight overlapping public sector jobs. He was contractually obliged to work full time and was paid a full-time salary by each organisation. He is accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000.
In March 2023 Chowdhury began working for the Home Office despite being under contract to work full time at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency.
The court was told he started the Home Office job while on sick leave from three of his other jobs.
Prosecuting barrister Lucy Organ asked him: "If you were really sick for work, how were you able to start your work at the Home Office?"
Chowdhury said: "I did not want this job at the Home Office, I was told there would be adequate support and I could work whatever hours I wanted to work."
Organ also asked why he did not submit a sick note to the Home Office "You were using these sick notes to be able to cope. It was all too much wasn't it?"
Chowdhury rejected the suggestion, adding: "I wanted to carry on working."
In May 2023, Chowdhury was contracted to work 183 hours a week, more than the number of hours in seven days.
He told the jury he agreed with his employers to work flexibly and that his work was project or output based. He said this was agreed "informally" via text messages but the phones used to send the texts had gone missing when his house was searched by investigators.
He said that to cope with the workload he would work from 07:00 on Saturdays and Sundays and not finish until 20:00 or 21:00.

- Published2 days ago
Organ asked him: "Wasn't that a bit much for you?"
"I was house bound, I was looking after my mum," he said.
The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity".
His line manager at the UKHSA, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him in May 2023 to discuss his sick leave.
She previously told the court she was surprised when he logged on wearing white make-up because his name led her to expect to see an Asian man with darker skin.
She told the court that as the meeting went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck."
But Chowdhury denied having worn make-up at the meeting
''That's a smear, I've never worn make-up in my life. At that particular time, I was suffering from anxiety and depression. I had already submitted my sick note, there was no need to put on make-up.''
The trial continues.

title: American Express is cutting 5% of its workforce to 'prepare for AI'
titleJa: American Express is cutting 5% of its workforce to 'prepare for AI'
summaryJa: Amex, which reported third-quarter results earlier Friday, is taking a $336 million restructuring charge in the quarter, CEO Stephen Squeri said Friday.
bodyOriginal:
American Express is cutting thousands of employees as the leading credit card company prepares for artificial intelligence to take over more of its internal processes.
Amex is eliminating 5% of its global workforce and taking a $336 million restructuring charge, CEO Stephen Squeri told analysts Friday on the company's third-quarter earnings call. The firm had almost 77,000 employees at the end of 2025.
Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC in an interview that the restructuring was to make American Express "leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI."
"You don't want to automate processes that are not optimally structured," Le Caillec said. "So what we're doing here is to reduce layers and increase spans of controls, so that we can automate and take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and the coming years."

title: France is flashing euro crisis signals. This time, the fault lines are different
titleJa: France is flashing euro crisis signals. This time, the fault lines are different
summaryJa: French borrowing costs have surged as debt and political risks mount, raising questions over whether the stress could spread across the euro zone.
bodyOriginal:
As France's economic and political woes mount, investors are asking whether the country's debt problems risk contaminating the rest of the euro zone.
Markets are flashing alarm bells over the euro zone's second-biggest economy. The euro has remained under pressure, falling almost 5% against the dollar since the start of the year.
France's benchmark borrowing cost, the yield on its 10-year bond, rose above 5% for the first time since 2002 this week before moving sharply higher.
Meanwhile, the spread between French and German 10-year bond yields — a closely watched metric of distress — reached more than 170 basis points on Thursday for the first time since the euro zone debt crisis of the early 2010s. The cost of insuring the French government against default, as measured by credit default swaps, is also the highest since that period.
Euro zone contagion
The big concern is fragmentation, when countries that share a currency face sharply different borrowing costs, compounding market stress and risking spiraling debt repayments for the worst-impacted countries.
As the euro zone sovereign debt crisis of the early 2010s showed, market stress in one country can spread rapidly through economies that share a currency and a central bank but retain separate fiscal systems. The crisis began in Greece before spreading to countries including Portugal, Ireland, Italy and Spain.
Governments were expected to rescue struggling banks, which held large amounts of sovereign debt, creating a vicious cycle.
The crisis only eased after rescue programs tied to sweeping austerity measures, and ECB President Mario Draghi pledged in 2012 to do "whatever it takes" to preserve the euro.
Economists are warning that a new vicious cycle is being created — not only in France but in big economies from the U.S. to the U.K. — as investor concern over rising government debt pushes up yields and interest costs, which in turn add to the debt burden.
A slowdown in bond purchases raises "the specter that the government will be forced into default because it simply doesn't have the cash to pay interest and principal on its debt," Nobel laureate Paul Krugman wrote in a blog on Oct. 8.
"Fear of default then leads to even more capital flight, which increases fears of default and the interest rate," he said.
France's debt risks
France in particular has one of the highest deficit-to-GDP ratios in the 21-nation euro area and a growing national debt pile. Its economy has slowed to a crawl, with the government cutting its 2026 growth forecast to just 0.5%.
Those fiscal strains come as political volatility and social unrest raise doubts about the government's ability to deliver measures aimed at stabilizing the public finances.
"We are deep into French crisis territory," Carsten Brzeski, ING's global head of macro research and chief euro zone economist, said by email.
"There is no risk of an imminent liquidity issue for the French government but the lack of trust of bond markets and the ongoing crisis should finally bring a high sense of urgency to Paris."
John Stopford, head of multi-asset income at Ninety One, said France has gone from being a core or semi-core European country for fixed income investors to increasingly being considered on the periphery, which he labeled "bizarre" given the history of France in relation to the EU and its economic power in the continent.
"We as investors, have just chosen for the time being to pretty much avoid all of the non-core countries in Europe – it's too fluid a situation with too much uncertainty to really want to get involved," Stopford said on a call.
Why 2026 is different
Nonetheless, analysts CNBC spoke to broadly agreed that reforms meant that even if the market is behaving in similar ways to the post-financial crisis period, the contagion risk remained limited this time around.
Ninety One's Stopford said spreads would likely need to be trading "in the 200s" before the situation is broadly perceived as a genuine crisis — but, he added, that the situation in France "doesn't look great."
"French spreads are now wider than they were at the peak of the peripheral crisis of the early 2010s, but they're still much narrower than the extreme levels that we saw in Spain, Italy, Greece and Ireland back then, so... I think the market's assumption is that things will need to get worse before we get to a point where EU institutions start to look to try and limit further damage," he told CNBC.
BlackRock strategists noted the current environment is "materially different" to the one that preceded the 2011 to 2012 euro zone debt crisis, with the region now better equipped to weather financial stress, but they added that "further volatility and spillovers remain possible."
"The French bond sell-off illustrates how competition for capital is reshaping fixed income markets amid a global rate reset," they wrote. "Rising government borrowing and AI-related investment are pushing up financing costs, exposing borrowers with deteriorating fundamentals to greater scrutiny."
George Lagarias, chief economist at Forvis Mazars, said France was already in a debt crisis, citing its debt-to-GDP ratio of 119% at the end of the second quarter of 2026 — close to Greece's of 128% in late 2009.
A spillover would mean a wider French-German yield spread followed by higher credit default swap prices – the cost of insuring debt, he said.
"Italy, Spain, would see higher borrowing costs, and have to curtail fiscal expenditures, possibly raising political backlash in their own countries," he told CNBC. "The European periphery would come under tremendous pressure, even if their finances are in much better order than a few years ago."
However, Lagarias said crucial structural differences minimize the risk of a wider spillover akin to the early 2010s, which he estimated at 10% to 20%.
"Greece had a very bad trade deficit. France also has a trade deficit, but the numbers are much more benign," he said by email.
He added that the Insee, France's national statistics body, was "not likely to lie about the deficit" and contrasted this with Greece.
In 2009, Greece sharply revised its projected budget deficit from 3.7% of GDP in the spring to 12.5% by October, undermining confidence in the reliability of its public finances and helping accelerate the crisis.
"[French] debt levels are worrying but known. Markets can deal with known risks. They hate surprises," Lagarias added. "What sunk Greece was a deficit that was suddenly revealed to be five-fold versus the official estimate. This catalysed a crisis."
Alex Everett, investment director for rates management at Aberdeen Investments, agreed that the current environment should be treated "primarily as French risk rather than a systemic euro-area risk."
"Compared to the early 2010s, the Eurozone has stronger banks, greater integration and numerous tools designed to limit the risk of sovereign fragmentation," he said. "I anticipate contagion to be short-lived."

title: U.S. oil holds above $100, Brent at five-month high as Iran says it’s prepared for warfare
titleJa: U.S. oil holds above $100, Brent at five-month high as Iran says it’s prepared for warfare
summaryJa: U.S. President Donald Trump accused Iran on Thursday of trying to manipulate the oil market.
bodyOriginal:
Crude oil futures ticked higher on Friday, with global benchmark Brent crude hovering at a five-month high.
By 6:51 a.m. ET, front-month Brent crude oil futures were 1.1% higher at $114.49 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were up 1.6% to trade at $101.04 a barrel.
Brent futures were on track for a weekly rise of 3.3%, putting the contracts on course for their third consecutive week of gains. They were also trading at their highest since early May.
WTI futures were on track for a weekly decline of 1.1%, putting the contracts on course to snap two consecutive weeks of gains.
Traders are continuing to monitor developments in the Middle East.
On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump accused Iran of lying about attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," he wrote on Truth Social. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."
Iran's Islamic Revolution Guards Corps said Thursday that four vessels had been struck and caught fire in the Persian Gulf, according to the Iranian state-affiliated Tasnim news agency, while a further three had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
Separately, Iran's army chief was reported to have said the country's military is fully prepared for "asymmetric warfare" after strengthening its capabilities.
In Saudi Arabia, oil giant Saudi Aramco reportedly told staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely following a series of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Reuters reported.
The Houthis have launched strikes on Saudi airports and some Aramco offices in recent weeks, resulting in multiple fatalities.

title: Earnings limit of up to £140K for first-time buyers loan scheme
titleJa: Earnings limit of up to £140K for first-time buyers loan scheme
summaryJa: The Your First Home scheme will offer government-backed loans for those buying new-builds in England.
bodyOriginal:
Earnings limit of up to £140K for first-time buyers loan scheme
- Published
The government is expected to allow households earning up to £110,000 to apply for its new loan scheme to help first-time buyers in England.
As first reported by The Times, external, a higher earnings limit of £140,000 is expected to apply to those purchasing properties in London.
The Your First Home scheme will offer government-backed equity loans worth 20% of new-build properties purchased from participating developers.
The loans, which will also be subject to an initial interest-free period, are designed to help people buy a home with deposits as low as 2.5%.
Previous schemes to help first-time buyers did not restrict eligibility by income but faced criticism for stoking house prices by allowing relatively wealthy households to borrow more.
Unveiling the Your First Home Scheme at last month's Labour conference, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it would focus on those who "really need support".
Details of the changes, including salary caps, are due to be confirmed at next week's Budget.
The Times reported that ministers had initially decided to set the earnings limits at £90,000 for homes outside outside London and £110,000 in the capital, before concluding this would deny access to too many middle-earning couples, such as teachers and nurses.
The government has also argued that the scheme will help to boost housebuilding, after ministers conceded they are set to miss a target to build 1.5 million homes in England by the next election.
Help to Buy
Labour has said the scheme will be funded by within existing government budgets, but is yet to provide details of which other areas will see their spending cut.
Developers taking part in the scheme will also be asked to contribute towards running costs.
Like the Help to Buy scheme launched under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, the scheme will use equity loans, which are linked to changes in the value of properties they are used to purchase.
That scheme, which initially ran between 2013 and 2021, enabled all home purchasers to put down a 5% deposit on a newly built home worth up to £600,000.
Up to 20% of the cost of the home was funded by a shared equity loan, which was interest-free for the first five years.
A second version of that scheme, which ran from 2021 to 2023, restricted access to first-time buyers and applied regional-level price caps to the properties could be bought under the programme.
